pos: n. (Granville Sharp, 1735–1813, English abolitionist and Greek grammarian, first chairman of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade)
etymology: English surname Sharp, from the adjective, keen; Granville, from a Norman place name.
biblical_def: Granville Sharp was a linen-draper's apprentice turned clerk in the Ordnance Office who taught himself Greek, Hebrew, and law, and used all three. In 1765 he found a beaten slave, Jonathan Strong, on a London street, had him treated, and when the owner seized him again fought the case; he then spent seven years on the law until in 1772 the Somerset case established that a slave could not be forcibly carried out of England. He was the first chairman of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in 1787 and a founder of the Sierra Leone settlement and of the British and Foreign Bible Society. His Remarks on the Uses of the Definitive Article in the Greek Text of the New Testament (1798) established the grammatical rule that bears his name, by which Tit 2:13 and 2Pe 1:1 name Jesus Christ as “the great God and our Saviour” (Tit 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the article as a part of speech used before nouns to limit their signification, and habeas corpus as a writ for delivering a person from false imprisonment.
webster_full: AR'TICLE, n. In grammar, a part of speech used before nouns to limit or define their application; as the English a, an, the.
HA'BEAS COR'PUS. A writ for delivering a person from false imprisonment, or for removing a person from one court to another.
EMANCIPA'TION, n. The act of setting free from servitude or slavery; deliverance from bondage.
scriptures: Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ, to them that have obtained like precious faith with us through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ:
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
corruption_summary: The man who freed slaves in English courts also proved from the Greek article that Christ is called God.
corruption_paragraphs: Sharp's rule is a real contribution and the dictionary states it precisely: where two singular personal nouns of the same case are joined by kai and the article stands before the first only, both describe one person. Applied to Tit 2:13 and 2Pe 1:1 the construction yields the plain sense that “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13) is one subject, not two, so that the texts are direct assertions of the Saviour's deity. The rule was attacked at the time by Unitarian writers for exactly that reason and has stood.

The two halves of his life come from one doctrine. Act 17:26 teaches that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26), and Exo 21:16 sentences the manstealer; a man who believes those texts and reads Greek will end up in both the courtroom and the grammar. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Sharp himself, though the rule is sometimes dismissed as a piece of apologetic convenience. It was published by a man with no academic post who had already spent twenty years losing money on lawsuits for other people's freedom, which is not the profile of a special pleader.
usage: “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13) — one subject, by his rule.
“the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (2Pe 1:1) — the same construction.
“hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26) — why he went to court.

pos: n. (James Ramsay, 1733–1789, naval surgeon turned Anglican priest in St Kitts, first insider witness against West Indian slavery)
etymology: Scottish surname Ramsay, from a place name, the ram's island or wild-garlic island.
biblical_def: James Ramsay was a Scottish naval surgeon who in 1759 was ordered aboard a slave ship with an epidemic on it, and never recovered from what he saw between decks. He took orders and served parishes in St Kitts for nineteen years, where he attempted to catechize and baptize the enslaved and was boycotted by his own planter vestries for it. He came home and in 1784 published An Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies, the first detailed account of the system by a man who had administered sacraments inside it. The planter interest answered with pamphlets attacking his character, and he spent his last five years supplying Wilberforce and the Commons committees with evidence, dying in 1789 in the middle of the fight. Jer 22:13 names the thing he described, the man who “useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a planter as one who owns a plantation, and testimony as a solemn declaration made for establishing some fact.
webster_full: PLANT'ER, n. One who plants, sets, introduces or establishes; one who owns a plantation; used in the West Indies and Southern states of America.
TES'TIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
MEN'STEALER, n. One who steals men; one who kidnaps.
scriptures: Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
Phm 1:16
Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?
Mat 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
corruption_summary: Nineteen years inside the system, one book, and five years of being called a liar for writing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Ramsay's evidence was decisive because it was not hearsay. He had buried the dead, attempted the catechism, and been obstructed by the men whose interest it was; and he could answer the planters' standard defences from inside. 1Ti 1:10 puts menstealers in the list of the lawless, and Phm 1:16 shows Paul returning a runaway as “a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16), which is the relation the colonial church could not maintain and a slave code cannot allow.

The corruption to name is the use of the parish church as an instrument of the estate. Ramsay's vestries did not object to religion; they objected to a religion administered to the enslaved on the same terms as to themselves, because a sacrament implies a soul and a soul implies a brother. Mat 5:11 is what he received for pressing it, men saying “all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11). He died before the trade was touched and the men who carried it had his papers.
usage: “useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13) — the system he described.
“a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16) — the relation a slave code forbids.
“shall say all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11) — his last five years.

pos: n. (Thomas Clarkson, 1760–1846, English abolitionist, chief gatherer of evidence against the slave trade)
etymology: English patronymic Clark-son, son of the clerk.
biblical_def: Thomas Clarkson won a Cambridge Latin essay prize in 1785 on the question whether it is lawful to make men slaves against their will, and the research he did for it took over his life. He became the evidence-gatherer of the abolition movement, riding by his own count some thirty-five thousand miles through the ports of Bristol, Liverpool, and London, boarding ships, interviewing sailors, surgeons, and captains, and assembling the depositions on which the parliamentary case rested. He carried a chest of African manufactures — cloth, carved work, dyes, produce — to prove that the continent had trade to offer besides men, and he circulated the plan of the slave ship Brookes which showed the stowage to scale. Pro 31:8 is the commission he worked under, to “Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deposition as the testimony of a witness reduced to writing, and evidence as that which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth.
webster_full: DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of giving testimony under oath; the attested written testimony of a witness.
EV'IDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions, or from the testimony of others.
TRAF'FIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling; commodities of trade.
scriptures: Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
Psa 82:3
Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
corruption_summary: Thirty-five thousand miles of interviews, a chest of African goods, and a ship's plan drawn to scale.
corruption_paragraphs: Clarkson's method is worth study by anyone who wants to see a wrong ended rather than deplored. He did not argue the principle, which Wilberforce argued in the House; he established the facts, in such volume and with such specificity that the trade's defenders could not maintain their account of it. Eph 5:11 commands not fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness “but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11), and the Greek carries the sense of exposing to light, which is what a deposition does.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Pro 31:8 requires a voice for those who have none, and that supplying such a voice is mostly clerical labour: travel, note-taking, cross-checking, and years of it. Isa 58:6 names the end, to “let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6). Clarkson lived to see both the trade abolished in 1807 and slavery itself in the British empire in 1833, which few reformers of any cause are given.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'illem (H483), dumb, mute; chophshi (H2670), free; Greek elegcho (G1651), to reprove, expose.
roots_lines: Greek elegcho (G1651) — to reprove, expose to light; Ephesians 5:11.
usage: “Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8) — his commission for sixty years.
“but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11) — exposure to light, which is what evidence is.
“let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — and he lived to see it twice.

pos: n. (Zachary Macaulay, 1768–1838, Clapham abolitionist, governor of Sierra Leone, editor of the Christian Observer)
etymology: Hebrew Zekaryah, the LORD has remembered; Gaelic MacAmhlaidh, son of Olaf.
biblical_def: Zachary Macaulay went out at sixteen as a bookkeeper and then manager on a Jamaica sugar estate, and what he administered there turned him for life. He came home, joined the Clapham circle, served as governor of Sierra Leone from 1794, and was captured by the French in the course of it; he then edited the Christian Observer for fourteen years and became the movement's statistician. His particular gift was the mastery of detail: he compiled and verified the returns, the shipping records, and the colonial registries, and it was Macaulay the committees sent for when a planter's figures needed testing. He worked on the registration of slaves as the means of exposing the illegal trade after 1807. He was the father of the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay. Job 31:15 is the question he carried out of Jamaica, “Did not he that made me in the womb make him?” (Job 31:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a registry as a book in which a record is kept, and an overseer as one who superintends others.
webster_full: REG'ISTRY, n. The act of recording or writing in a register; the book or record in which entries are made.
OVERSEE'R, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; an officer who has the care of the poor.
ESTATE', n. The interest or quantity of interest a man has in lands; property; fortune; a plantation.
scriptures: Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
corruption_summary: He managed a sugar estate at twenty and spent the next forty years dismantling the system he had run.
corruption_paragraphs: Macaulay is the Clapham figure whose conversion to the cause was not theoretical. He had kept the books and given the orders, and he knew precisely which of the planters' published assurances were false and how to prove it. Job 31:15 is the text that undoes the whole apparatus of justification at a stroke, since a common Maker in the womb leaves no room for a difference of kind between the overseer and the overseen.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sanctified use of tedium. Macaulay's contribution was columns of verified figures, maintained for decades, and without them the parliamentary speeches would have been sentiment. Exo 21:16 supplied the law and Pro 31:8 the duty; the registries supplied the proof that the law was being broken on a scale the trade's defenders denied. Isa 58:6 is what the figures were for.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asah (H6213), to make; beten (H990), the womb; ganab (H1589), to steal.
usage: “Did not he that made me in the womb make him?” (Job 31:15) — what he brought back from Jamaica.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — the law his registries proved broken.
“Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8) — in his case, in columns of figures.

pos: n. (James Stephen, 1758–1832, barrister and Master in Chancery, legal strategist of the abolition of the slave trade)
etymology: Greek Stephanos, a crown; the surname is patronymic.
biblical_def: James Stephen practised law in St Kitts as a young man, saw a trial of four slaves there which he never forgot, and came home a convinced abolitionist. He became a Master in Chancery and an MP, married Wilberforce's sister, and settled at Clapham. His contribution was strategic rather than rhetorical. War in Disguise; or, the Frauds of the Neutral Flags (1805) argued that neutral shipping was carrying enemy colonial trade in breach of maritime law; the argument persuaded the government to act against neutral carriers, and Stephen then drafted the Foreign Slave Trade Act of 1806, which prohibited British subjects and ships from supplying slaves to foreign and conquered colonies. It passed as a war measure with little opposition, and it destroyed perhaps two-thirds of the British trade before the abolition of 1807 was ever voted. Amo 5:24 is the demand his method served, that judgment “run down as waters” (Amo 5:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chancery as a court of equity, and a neutral as a nation or state which takes no part in a contest between others.
webster_full: CHAN'CERY, n. In Great Britain, the highest court of justice next to the parliament; a court of equity.
NEU'TRAL, n. A person or nation that takes no part in a contest between others; the state of being unengaged.
STAT'UTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state that extends its binding force to all the citizens or subjects of that state.
scriptures: Amo 5:24
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Pro 31:9
Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
corruption_summary: He killed most of the slave trade with a wartime shipping statute before anyone voted to abolish it.
corruption_paragraphs: Stephen's 1806 Act is the least celebrated and perhaps the most effective single step in the whole abolition campaign, and it is a lesson in how righteousness is actually enacted. Twenty years of moral argument had failed to carry a general abolition; a narrowly drawn statute, framed as a measure of economic warfare against France, passed almost unnoticed and removed the larger part of the traffic. Mic 6:8 requires doing justly as well as loving mercy, and doing is a matter of drafting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the man who finds the lawful instrument serves the cause as truly as the man who makes the speech, and usually gets none of the credit. Pro 31:9 commands judging righteously and pleading the cause of the poor and needy, and Stephen did it in the form of a bill. Exo 21:16 was the standing law behind it; his work was to make English statute reach the ships that were breaking it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpat (H4941), judgment; tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness; din (H1777), to plead a cause.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — what the LORD requires; Micah 6:8.
usage: “let judgment run down as waters” (Amo 5:24) — by statute, as it happens.
“to do justly, and to love mercy” (Mic 6:8) — the doing is a drafting problem.
“plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9) — he pleaded it in a bill.

pos: n. (John Thornton, 1720–1790, Clapham merchant and the chief Evangelical philanthropist of his generation)
etymology: English surname Thornton, from a place name, the thorn-bush settlement.
biblical_def: John Thornton was a Russia merchant and a director of the Bank of England, reckoned one of the richest commoners in England, and he gave away most of what he had. His giving was systematic rather than impulsive. He bought advowsons — the legal right of presentation to parishes — in order to place preaching ministers in pulpits that would otherwise have gone to men who did not preach, and he maintained a large private correspondence and pension list among poor clergy. He brought John Newton from Olney to St Mary Woolnoth in London and supported him there. He funded Bibles and tracts, subsidised the evangelical press, and paid for the education of ministers' sons. His house at Clapham became the gathering place of the circle his son Henry and William Wilberforce afterwards made famous. Mat 25:40 is the reckoning his accounts were kept by.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an advowson as the right of presentation to a church or benefice, and a benefactor as one who confers a benefit.
webster_full: ADVOW'SON, n. In English law, a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice; the right of nominating a person to officiate in a vacant church.
BENEFAC'TOR, n. He that confers a benefit, commonly one who makes charitable contributions.
STEW'ARD, n. A man employed to manage the affairs of another; one who is entrusted with the management of another's property.
scriptures: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Gal 2:10
Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:
corruption_summary: He bought the right to appoint ministers so that parishes would hear preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The buying of advowsons looks strange to a modern reader and was the most practical thing Thornton did. Patronage was a property right; if it was going to be exercised by somebody, an evangelical merchant could exercise it as lawfully as an absentee landlord, and the parishes got sermons. The arrangement is not the New Testament pattern, and the dictionary says so in the entry on the Veto Act; within a system of established patronage, Thornton used the instrument that existed. 1Ti 5:18 is the ground on which he paid poor clergy, that “The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the systematic character of his giving. Gal 2:10 records the apostolic instruction to remember the poor, and Thornton did it by list, by correspondence, and by standing arrangement, not by occasional generosity. Mat 25:40 makes the whole of it a service rendered to Christ in “one of the least of these my brethren” (Mat 25:40), which is why he did not advertise it and why the sums were only discovered afterwards.
usage: “one of the least of these my brethren” (Mat 25:40) — how he kept his accounts.
“they would that we should remember the poor” (Gal 2:10) — by list and standing order.
“The labourer is worthy of his reward” (1Ti 5:18) — the ground for pensioning clergy.

pos: n. (Henry Thornton, 1760–1815, banker, monetary theorist, member of Parliament, and treasurer of the Clapham societies)
etymology: English surname Thornton, the thorn-bush settlement; Henry, from Germanic, home-ruler.
biblical_def: Henry Thornton was the son of John Thornton, a partner in the bank of Down, Thornton and Free, and member of Parliament for Southwark for thirty-three years. He was the Clapham circle's man of business: treasurer of the Church Missionary Society and of the British and Foreign Bible Society, a director of the Sierra Leone Company, and the keeper of the accounts for the abolition campaign. His house at Battersea Rise, with the library Pitt helped design, was where the circle met and where Wilberforce lodged for years. He was also a serious economist: An Enquiry into the Nature and Effects of the Paper Credit of Great Britain (1802) is a founding work of monetary theory, and he drafted much of the Bullion Report of 1810. He is said to have given away six-sevenths of his income before his marriage and a third of it afterwards. 2Co 9:7 is the rule, that “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines credit as trust given or received, the reputation of solvency, and a treasurer as one who has the care of a treasure or of money collected.
webster_full: CRED'IT, n. Trust; confidence; a trusting to, or placing confidence in; reputation of solvency, which entitles a man to be trusted.
TREAS'URER, n. One who has the care of a treasure or treasury; an officer who receives the public money arising from taxes and duties.
CUR'RENCY, n. Circulation; a passing from hand to hand; the whole amount of money or paper in circulation as a medium of trade.
scriptures: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
Mal 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: The man who wrote the founding book on paper credit gave away most of what passed through his hands.
corruption_paragraphs: Thornton is the answer to the notion that financial competence and liberality belong to different temperaments. He understood money better than almost anyone in England — his analysis of how a note issue, a bullion drain, and a harvest failure interact was a century ahead of the Bank's own thinking — and he treated his own income as a fund held in trust. 1Co 16:2 describes the method, laying by in store “as God hath prospered him” (1Co 16:2), proportionate and regular rather than occasional.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the keeping of books for other people's causes. Someone has to be treasurer of a missionary society, and the work is invisible, unthanked, and the thing that makes the rest possible; Thornton did it for two of the largest societies in Britain at once while sitting in Parliament and writing on currency. Mat 25:21 is the only commendation such work is promised, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21), spoken to a steward.
roots_summary: Greek hilaros (G2431), cheerful; thesaurizo (G2343), to lay up in store; oikonomos (G3623), a steward.
roots_lines: Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up, store; 1 Corinthians 16:2.
usage: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7) — a third of a banker's income.
“as God hath prospered him” (1Co 16:2) — proportionate and regular.
“Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21) — a treasurer's only wage.

pos: n. (Thomas Babington, 1758–1837, of Rothley Temple, member of Parliament and Clapham abolitionist)
etymology: English surname Babington, from a Northumberland place name, Babba's settlement.
biblical_def: Thomas Babington of Rothley Temple in Leicestershire was member of Parliament for Leicester for eighteen years and one of the steadiest members of the Clapham circle. He married Zachary Macaulay's sister and gave the young Macaulay his start; the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay carries his name. He was a director of the Sierra Leone Company, a founder of the Church Missionary Society and of the British and Foreign Bible Society, and the man to whom the circle habitually gave the unglamorous committee work. At Rothley he reorganised the parish relief of the poor and the village school on his own account. He also took on the Society for the Reformation of Prison Discipline and the campaign against the lottery. Jas 1:27 defines what his working life consisted of, visiting “the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a committee as one or more persons elected to examine or manage any matter, and relief as the removal of pain or distress.
webster_full: COMMIT'TEE, n. One or more persons, elected or appointed, to whom any matter or business is referred, either by a legislative body, or by a court.
RELIEF', n. The removal, in whole or in part, of any evil that pains the body or distresses the mind; alleviation of pain or distress.
PHILAN'THROPY, n. Love to mankind; benevolence towards the whole human family; universal good will.
scriptures: Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Gal 2:10
Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do.
Psa 82:3
Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
Act 4:34
Neither was there any among them that lacked: for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold,
corruption_summary: The Clapham man who took the committee work nobody wanted, for fifty years.
corruption_paragraphs: Every reforming circle needs one Babington: the member who sits on the committee, reads the papers, checks the accounts, and is never quoted. He did it for abolition, for the two great societies, for prison discipline, and for his own Leicestershire parish at the same time. Psa 82:3 commands the defence of the poor and fatherless and the doing of “justice to the afflicted and needy” (Psa 82:3), which in a settled country mostly takes the form of administration.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the local half of his work. Act 4:34 describes a church in which “there any among them that lacked” was not the case, because possessions were turned into relief, and Babington ran the equivalent in one village while legislating at Westminster. Gal 2:10 attaches remembering the poor to apostolic fellowship itself. A reform movement whose members are generous at a distance and absent from their own parish has got the order wrong, and Clapham on the whole did not.
roots_summary: Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to visit, look after; orphanos (G3737), fatherless; Hebrew 'ani (H6041), afflicted.
roots_lines: Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, look after; James 1:27.
usage: “the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — his working life.
“do justice to the afflicted and needy” (Psa 82:3) — mostly, administration.
“Neither was there any among them that lacked” (Act 4:34) — the village as well as the empire.

pos: n. (Charles Grant, 1746–1823, East India Company director and chairman, author of the pious clause opening India to missionaries)
etymology: Scottish surname Grant, from Norman French grand, great.
biblical_def: Charles Grant was a Highlander who went to Bengal as a young man, made a fortune, lost children to smallpox, and was converted there. He returned to London, rose to be a director and three times chairman of the East India Company, and sat in Parliament for Inverness-shire. The Company's settled policy was to exclude missionaries from its territories on the ground that preaching endangered trade and order. Grant worked against that policy for twenty years from inside the Company itself: he wrote Observations on the State of Society among the Asiatic Subjects of Great Britain, pressed the case in 1793 and failed, and in 1813, when the charter came up again, carried with Wilberforce the clauses that admitted missionaries and provided for an ecclesiastical establishment in India. He was also a founder of the Church Missionary Society. Mat 28:19 is the commission he spent two decades making legally possible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charter as a written instrument conferring rights and privileges, and a missionary as one sent to propagate religion.
webster_full: CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; one sent on a mission.
COM'PANY, n. An association of persons for the purpose of carrying on some commercial or industrial undertaking.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.
corruption_summary: A chairman of the East India Company spent twenty years getting missionaries past his own Company's policy.
corruption_paragraphs: The Company's exclusion of missionaries is a clean example of commercial interest setting the limits of the gospel's advance. The argument was always prudential: preaching would offend, offence would disturb, disturbance would cost. Mar 16:15 does not admit the qualification — “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — and Mat 24:14 says the gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness to all nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Grant, though the whole subject of missions under empire is now commonly read as a single colonial enterprise. The dictionary distinguishes them, and Grant's career is the reason it can: the commercial power and the missionary cause were on opposite sides of this question for twenty years, and the Company had to be beaten in Parliament before a missionary could land lawfully. Act 1:8 sets the witness from Jerusalem to the uttermost part of the earth, and in 1813 the obstacle was a trading charter.

“teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — what the charter had excluded.
“unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8) — the obstacle was a trading company.

pos: n. (William Goode, 1762–1816, rector of St Andrew-by-the-Wardrobe, secretary of the Eclectic Society and a founder of the Church Missionary Society)
etymology: English surname Goode, from the adjective, or from Old English Goda, a personal name.
biblical_def: William Goode was curate and then successor to William Romaine at St Andrew-by-the-Wardrobe and Blackfriars in the City of London, where he preached for a quarter of a century. He was secretary of the Eclectic Society, the clerical discussion circle at which the question “What methods can we use more effectually to promote the knowledge of the gospel among the heathen?” was debated in 1796 and out of which the Church Missionary Society was founded in 1799; Goode was one of its founders and its early secretaries. He published An Entire New Version of the Book of Psalms, a metrical psalter in two volumes intended for congregational use, and a volume of essays on the Psalms. He was also one of the London clergy who maintained the evangelical cause in the City when it had few pulpits there. Psa 96:3 is the sentence the Eclectic Society's question was an application of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation, and metrical as pertaining to measure, or consisting of verse.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; the rendering of a passage or a book from one language into another.
MET'RICAL, a. Pertaining to measure, or metre; consisting of verses; as metrical compositions.
SO'CIETY, n. A number of persons united, either for business or pleasure, in a single company or interest.

Psa 67:2
That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations.
corruption_summary: He kept the minutes of the society that founded the Church Missionary Society, and versified the Psalms.
corruption_paragraphs: The Eclectic Society was a dozen London clergymen meeting in a vestry to discuss questions, and it produced the largest Anglican missionary society in the world. The question it put in 1796 was practical rather than theoretical — not whether the heathen should be evangelised but by what methods it could be done more effectually — and the answer was an organised society with funds, candidates, and committees. Psa 96:3 is the command underneath it, “Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing in Goode's own output. The same man who organised a missionary society spent years putting the Psalms into English metre so that a City congregation could sing them, because Isa 52:7 and Psa 67:2 are both sung and obeyed. A missionary movement detached from the ordinary worship of the sending churches runs on enthusiasm; one grown out of congregations singing the Psalms about the nations has roots.
roots_summary: Hebrew caphar (H5608), to recount, declare; goy (H1471), nation, heathen; basar (H1319), to bring tidings.
usage: “Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the Eclectic Society's question in brief.
“that publisheth peace” (Isa 52:7) — what a psalter is for as well as a society.
“thy saving health among all nations” (Psa 67:2) — sung, then organised.
